newsitem.title: USA: Clinton dedicates memorial to "happy warrior" FDR.
newsitem.headline: Clinton dedicates memorial to "happy warrior" FDR.

text.p: President Bill Clinton opened a grand memorial to Franklin D. Roosevelt among Washington's hallowed monuments on Friday, saying it would enshrine him as the "happy warrior keeping America's rendezvous with destiny."

Dedication of the seven-acre memorial had been threatened by controversy over whether Roosevelt, the partially paralysed 32nd president who led the nation through the Depression and World War II, should be depicted in a wheelchair.

But plans by some disabled groups to disrupt the event with protests melted away after Clinton recently agreed to ask Congress to add a statue to the park portraying FDR -- whose legs were paralysed by polio -- in a wheelchair.

Only a small gaggle of cheerful activists in wheelchairs showed up Friday to wave signs thanking Clinton for his intervention. Nearby three members of a Florida Jewish group waved placards charging "FDR allowed the Holocaust".
The only real disruptions came every few minutes when an airplane on its way to or from National Airport flew low over the gathering in the lush greenery of West Potomac Park.
While noisy, the setting placed Roosevelt among the presidential giants of U.S. history -- Washington, Lincoln and Jefferson -- who have monuments nearby in the heart of the capital.

"This memorial will be the embodiment of FDR's faith, for it will ensure that all future generations will know," Clinton said. "It will ensure that they will all see the happy warrior, keeping America's rendezvous with destiny."

Although the main statue of FDR in the memorial has him looking rather serious, Clinton saw his infectious smile and optimism as key attributes of the man he called "the greatest president of this great American century."
"He electrified the nation, instilling confidence with every tilt of his head and boom of his laugh," Clinton told a crowd estimated by memorial officials as over five thousand.

It was FDR's faith in Americans that inspired them to do their part in the war effort, "gathering scrap, giving up nylons and eventually storming the beaches at Normandy and Okinawa and Anzio," Clinton said.

"It was that faith in his own extraordinary potential that enabled him to guide his country from a wheelchair. And from that wheelchair and a few halting steps, leaning on his sons' arms or those of trusted aides, he lifted a great people back to their feet and set America to march again ..."
If Roosevelt were alive today, he would have "great impatience and disdain" for many of the doubts that plague Americans today, Clinton said.
The ceremony was held at the entrance to the memorial, a large outdoor gallery of sculpture, waterfalls and granite walls carved with FDR quotations.

The $48 million park honours not just Roosevelt -- who had requested that any monument be limited to the size of his desk -- but his era. It includes figures standing in bread lines in the Depression and listening to FDR give his radio chats.

There is a sculpture of Eleanor Roosevelt, whom Clinton called FDR's "magnificent" partner, "his eyes and his ears" and conscience. There is even a statue of their Scottish terrier Fala, also shown in colouring books available at a gift shop.

Clinton, who is still recovering from surgery to his right knee, delivered his speech on crutches to a crowd including some two-dozen members of the Roosevelt family, who had been split over the correct way to deal with FDR's disability.
One of them, David B. Roosevelt, a member of the memorial comission, told the crowd, "The issues involved are complex and should not be surrendered to individual interests."

But another, Christopher duPont Roosevelt, told a reporter that with the added statue of FDR in a wheelchair, "I think it's going to end up right." The Senate has authorised money for the statue and the House is expected to follow suit soon.
FDR contracted polio at the age of 39, years before he entered the White House, and never walked again unaided. In public he sought to disguise his disability.
Harold Ickes, a former Clinton White House official and son of FDR's interior secretary, said his most vivid memory of FDR was seeing him being carried into the family farmhouse.
"I remember the people picking him up and bringing him in," said Ickes. "It made a real impression."
